title: When the Lantern Wakes
premise: In the fog-bound port city of Greyharbour, 1897, Oscar Yarrow has spent his life learning that survival means carrying only what you're told to carry. When an infant is abandoned at the trading company's door with a note ordering him to forget the face, Oscar instead recognizes the child as evidence of a smuggling ring trafficking indentured children — and that his own employer is at its heart. Armed with a ledger page and the baby's blanket, he must move both past three checkpoints before the company's enforcers burn the records at week's end. Betrayed by the mentor who raised him and aided by a customs officer with her own debts to the truth, Oscar delivers the evidence at terrible cost: the company falls, but the mentor dies buying him time, and Oscar leaves Greyharbour with the child, choosing loyalty to memory over the power that once promised him a name.
about_author: A. M. Iversen is the pen name of a former archivist who spent a decade cataloguing shipping manifests from northern port cities. Their fiction excavates the lives recorded only as cargo weights and initials.

chapters.title: The Weight of Small Things
chapters.summary: Oscar Yarrow, POV. A night dive for pearls gone wrong establishes Oscar's world: the Meridian Trading Company owns his debt, his hands, and his silence. When orders come to carry a sealed crate through the fog, he measures it by habit, not conscience. Emotional beat: numb competence masking a grief he refuses to name.

chapters.title: Left at the Door
chapters.summary: Still Oscar's POV. An infant appears on the company doorstep with a note in his supervisor's hand: forget the face. Oscar recognizes the blanket's weave as coming from the drowned village of Saltmere — a place the company claims never existed. Emotional beat: the first crack in obedience; forgetting suddenly feels like drowning.

chapters.title: What the Ledger Keeps
chapters.summary: POV shifts to Edith Crane, a customs officer drowning in her father's debts to Meridian. Filing manifests at midnight, she finds a page where forty names have been replaced by tonnage figures — all children, all bound inland. Emotional beat: dread curdling into resolve as she realizes her signature could bury or free them.

chapters.title: Three Checkpoints
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV. He maps his route: the harbor gate, the tollhouse, the customs hall — each guarded by men who know his face and his debt. His old mentor, Dree Halloway, teaches him the carriers' tricks of misdirection while watching him too closely. Emotional beat: warmth laced with suspicion; the lessons feel like rehearsals for betrayal.

chapters.title: The Face He Was Told to Forget
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV. The baby falls ill, forcing Oscar to shelter in Saltmere's ruins, where he finds matching blankets and a wall of carved children's initials. He understands: the child is someone's proof that Saltmere's people were sold, not lost at sea. Emotional beat: grief transmuted into purpose; the face will not be forgotten.

chapters.title: Halloway's Hand
chapters.summary: Dree Halloway's POV, revealed in flashback chapters interleaved with present action. We learn he helped traffic the children under coercion, and that leaving the baby was his one rebellion — and his trap. He reports Oscar's theft to buy his own pardon. Emotional beat: shame weaponized; love expressed as the cruelest protection.

chapters.title: Checkpoint One: The Harbor Gate
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV. With the ledger page sewn into the baby's swaddling, Oscar talks his way past the harbor gate using Dree's own misdirection — then spots Dree among the enforcers, pointing him out. Edith Crane intervenes, claiming jurisdiction over 'unmanifested cargo.' Emotional beat: terror sharpening into alliance; two liars telling the truth together.

chapters.title: Checkpoint Two: The Tollhouse Fire
chapters.summary: Oscar and Edith's alternating POV. Cornered at the tollhouse, they set a decoy fire to draw the enforcers while crossing the marsh with the child. Edith confesses her father sold Saltmere families to cover his debts. Emotional beat: mutual unmasking; trust built not on innocence but on shared guilt.

chapters.title: Checkpoint Three: The Customs Hall
chapters.summary: Climax. Oscar's POV. Dree intercepts them at the final door, blade drawn, ordered to erase the last witness. Instead he turns on the enforcers, buying Oscar seconds to reach Edith's desk and file the true manifest under seal. Dree falls; the record locks into place as the company's men arrive too late. Emotional beat: sacrifice completing the arc of loyalty — truth finally carried all the way.

chapters.title: What Can Be Carried
chapters.summary: Resolution. Oscar's POV, months later. The Meridian Company collapses; its ledgers become public testimony, and Saltmere's survivors reclaim their names. Oscar, his debt voided, boards a coastal packet with the child — now named for Dree — leaving behind the city that measured him in what he could carry. Emotional beat: quiet release; memory kept is heavier than any crate, and worth it.
